newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Conasupo says not to import corn in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Conasupo says not to import corn in 1997.

text.p: Mexico's national staple food agency Conasupo will not need to import any corn this year and will not consider future imports until May, an agency spokesman said on Monday.

Mexico's import quota of U.S. yellow corn of 2.5 million tonnes was filled by companies this year, and Conasupo did not import any of the staple in 1997, said the spokesman, who declined to be named. The quota was set in the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), he said.

"Thanks to the good output of corn in the past two harvest cycles, added to the national purchases Conasupo will made in the next harvest cycle, the supply of the basic staple is guaranteed to cover national consumption needs," the agency said in a statement.

The spokesman told Reuters that Conasupo will buy domestic corn through the end of the 1997-1998 crop cycle in April. He added that Conasupo kept 200,000 tonnes of corn in storage from 1996 for consumption this year.
Conasupo is expected to supply about 1.9 million tonnes of corn to the nation's mammoth tortilla industry this year.

The agency is the body through which the government offers a floor price to corn farmers, then resells the grain to corn flour and tortilla industrialists at subsidized prices. Mexico's Agriculture Minister Francisco Labastida Ochoa also instructed local corn buyers to give preference to domestic corn over foreign imports, Conasupo said.
He told a recent board meeting of Conasupo to "support Mexican farmers in the selling of the crops they harvest beginning in October."
Mexico produced almost four million tonnes of corn in the 1996-1997 fall-winter season, according to government estimates. The country has imported U.S. corn for years to cover its consumption needs.
Corn is a key staple in Mexico for the corn-flour pancakes that are essential in the typical diet.
